questions.q: In the Nigerian legal system, which judicial officer presides over an inquest to determine the identity of a deceased person and the cause, time, and manner of sudden or unnatural death?
questions.explain: Under the Nigerian Coroners Law, a Coroner (usually a Magistrate) conducts a judicial inquiry or inquest into sudden, violent, unnatural, or custody-related deaths to establish the identity of the deceased and how, when, and where death occurred.

open.q: Name the judicial officer in Nigeria who presides over an inquest into sudden, violent, or unnatural deaths.

questions.q: Under Nigerian law, which of the following deaths mandatorily requires notification to the Coroner for a medico-legal investigation?
options: Death of a 78-year-old patient in hospital after 3 weeks of documented metastatic cancer care
Death of an inmate while detained in police custody
Death of a neonate from prematurity after 10 days in a neonatal intensive care unit
Death of an elderly hypertensive patient at home under regular physician attendance
questions.explain: Any death occurring in police custody, prison, or psychiatric detention is a mandatory reportable death to the Coroner regardless of apparent natural cause, to rule out neglect, abuse, or foul play.

open.q: Why must the death of a detainee in police custody always be reported to the Coroner even if it appears to have a natural cause?
accept: To rule out foul play or neglect in custody
Deaths in custody require a coroner inquest

questions.q: Which standard of proof is required to establish guilt in a Nigerian criminal trial, such as a prosecution for murder or manslaughter?
questions.explain: Criminal trials require proof beyond reasonable doubt because conviction carries penal sanctions, whereas civil negligence claims are decided on a balance of probabilities.

open.q: What legal standard of proof is required to convict an accused person in a criminal trial?

questions.sub: Diagnosis of Death and Brain Death
questions.q: What is the single most critical prerequisite before initiating clinical brainstem death testing in a deeply comatose patient on a ventilator?
options: Presence of fixed dilated pupils for 6 hours
Exclusion of reversible causes of coma such as hypothermia and sedative drugs
Obtaining written consent from the hospital chief medical director
questions.explain: Before testing brainstem reflexes or performing an apnoea test, clinicians must establish an irreversible structural brain lesion and exclude confounding reversible factors including hypothermia, metabolic/endocrine disturbances, neuromuscular blockers, and central nervous system depressants.

open.q: What essential clinical condition must be excluded before performing brainstem death testing in a ventilated comatose patient?

questions.sub: Diagnosis of Death and Brain Death
questions.q: During an apnoea test to confirm brainstem death, the patient is disconnected from mechanical ventilation while receiving 100% oxygen via tracheal catheter. What arterial blood gas finding confirms an adequate respiratory stimulus without spontaneous breathing effort?
options: PaCO2 rising above 60 mmHg (8.0 kPa) with absent respiratory movements
PaO2 falling below 50 mmHg (6.7 kPa) with bradycardia
Arterial pH rising above 7.50 with chest wall excursion
PaCO2 falling below 25 mmHg (3.3 kPa) with gasping
questions.explain: An apnoea test demonstrates medullary respiratory centre unresponsiveness when hypercarbia (PaCO2 > 60 mmHg or a rise of > 20 mmHg above baseline, with pH < 7.30) fails to trigger any respiratory effort.

open.q: What arterial carbon dioxide threshold must be exceeded during an apnoea test to confirm maximal stimulation of the medullary respiratory centre?
accept: Rise in PaCO2 of more than 20 mmHg above baseline

questions.sub: Diagnosis of Death and Brain Death
questions.q: Which cranial nerve reflex is tested by instilling ice-cold water into the external auditory canal and observing for absent eye deviation during brainstem death assessment?
questions.explain: Caloric testing evaluates the vestibulo-ocular reflex (cranial nerves VIII, III, and VI); in brainstem death, irrigation of each tympanic membrane with ice-cold water produces no ocular movement.

open.q: Name the brainstem reflex tested by irrigating the external auditory canal with ice-cold water during brain death examination.

questions.q: Which early post-mortem change is characterized by progressive cooling of the corpse until it equilibrates with the ambient environmental temperature?
questions.explain: Algor mortis is the post-mortem cooling of the body following cessation of metabolic heat production and thermoregulation. Rigor mortis is muscular stiffening, and livor mortis is gravitational blood pooling.

open.q: Name the early post-mortem change characterized by cooling of the body to match ambient environmental temperature.

questions.q: A body is discovered at a crime scene with bright cherry-red post-mortem hypostasis (livor mortis) over the dependent posterior trunk. Which toxic exposure most commonly produces this colour of lividity?
questions.explain: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, which has a bright cherry-red hue reflected in dependent post-mortem hypostasis. Cyanide poisoning and severe cold exposure can also produce pink or bright red lividity.

open.q: Which common inhaled poison produces bright cherry-red post-mortem hypostasis due to carboxyhaemoglobin formation?

questions.q: At autopsy, a corpse exhibits fixed post-mortem hypostasis on the anterior chest and abdomen, even though police found the body lying supine on its back. What does this finding indicate?
options: The body was moved after hypostasis had already become fixed
The deceased died from acute massive pulmonary embolism
Death occurred less than 30 minutes before police arrival
The deceased suffered severe ante-mortem hypothermia
questions.explain: Livor mortis forms in the lowest dependent parts of the body due to gravity and becomes fixed (non-blanching) after roughly 8 to 12 hours; anterior fixed lividity in a supine corpse proves the body lay prone for hours after death before being turned over.

open.q: What forensic conclusion is drawn when a corpse found lying supine exhibits fixed post-mortem lividity on its anterior surface?
accept: The body was moved after death
The body originally lay prone and was turned over after fixation

questions.q: What is the direct biochemical cause of rigor mortis in skeletal muscle after death?
options: Excessive synthesis of acetylcholine at the motor end plate
Rapid accumulation of glycogen in sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.explain: After death, anaerobic glycolysis ceases and ATP is depleted; without ATP to detach myosin heads from actin filaments or pump calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, permanent actomyosin cross-bridges lock the muscles in stiffness.

open.q: What direct intracellular biochemical event causes actin and myosin filaments to remain locked together during rigor mortis?

questions.q: How does cadaveric spasm (instantaneous rigor) differ from ordinary rigor mortis?
options: It occurs instantaneously at the moment of death in a group of contracted muscles
It begins only after putrefactive marbling has appeared
It is caused by bacterial gas production in subcutaneous tissue
It affects smooth muscle exclusively and spares the hands
questions.explain: Cadaveric spasm is a rare, immediate stiffening of specific voluntary muscles active at the moment of sudden violent or emotional death (such as a hand tightly clutching a weapon or weeds in drowning), bypassing the stage of primary flaccidity.

open.q: How does cadaveric spasm differ from typical rigor mortis in terms of onset and anatomical distribution?
accept: Occurs instantaneously at death in specific active muscles
Immediate localized stiffening without primary flaccidity

questions.q: What is typically the earliest external visible sign of putrefaction in a corpse lying in a warm climate?
options: Greenish discoloration of the skin over the right iliac fossa
Mummification of the fingertips and ears
questions.explain: Putrefaction usually first manifests externally as a greenish discoloration over the right iliac fossa because the caecum lies close to the anterior abdominal wall and harbours abundant bacteria that produce hydrogen sulphide, converting haemoglobin to sulphaemoglobin.

open.q: What is usually the first external visible sign of putrefaction on a corpse?
accept: Greenish discoloration of the right iliac fossa
Greenish skin discoloration over the caecum
Greenish discoloration of the lower right abdomen

questions.q: Which bacterium, normally residing in the human large intestine, plays the predominant role in initiating endogenous putrefaction after death?
questions.explain: Clostridium perfringens (formerly Clostridium welchii) proliferates rapidly in bowel tissues after death, producing lecithinase, collagenase, and abundant gases that drive tissue breakdown, marbling, and bloating.

open.q: Name the anaerobic intestinal bacterium primarily responsible for initiating endogenous putrefaction after death.

questions.q: Which modified late post-mortem change involves hydrolysis and hydrogenation of body fats into a greasy, yellowish-white, soap-like substance in damp, warm, anaerobic environments?
questions.explain: Adipocere (grave wax) forms when bacterial enzymes hydrolyze triglycerides into saturated fatty acids (palmitic and stearic acids) in moist, airless conditions such as submerged bodies or damp graves, preserving facial and wound features for months or years.

open.q: Name the soap-like modification of putrefaction formed by hydrolysis and hydrogenation of body fats in damp, anaerobic conditions.

questions.q: Which environmental conditions favour mummification over wet putrefaction in an unburied corpse?
options: Hot, dry atmosphere with free air circulation
Submersion in polluted tropical river water
Deep burial in wet clay soil
questions.explain: Mummification occurs when rapid dehydration and desiccation of tissues outpace bacterial putrefaction, classically in hot, arid, well-ventilated environments (or dry cold) where the skin becomes shrivelled, leathery, and dark brown.

open.q: What environmental conditions favour post-mortem mummification rather than wet putrefaction?
accept: Hot and dry air with ventilation
Dry heat and good air circulation

questions.q: A 30-year-old man is found dead in an apartment at 25 degrees Celsius. Examination reveals generalized rigor mortis throughout the jaw, neck, and all four limbs, with fixed posterior livor mortis and no green abdominal discoloration. What is the most likely post-mortem interval?
questions.explain: In temperate-to-warm conditions, rigor mortis becomes fully established across all muscles by around 12 hours and persists up to 24–36 hours before secondary flaccidity sets in, while hypostasis fixes around 8–12 hours prior to visible putrefaction.

open.q: What approximate post-mortem interval is indicated by fully established generalized rigor mortis and fixed livor mortis without visible putrefaction?

questions.q: Which biochemical analyte measured in vitreous humour rises progressively and linearly after death, making it useful for estimating the post-mortem interval during the first 24 to 48 hours?
questions.explain: Vitreous humour is protected from rapid bacterial contamination; as retinal and choroidal cell membranes break down after death, intracellular potassium leaks steadily into the vitreous fluid at a predictable rate.

open.q: Name the electrolyte measured in post-mortem vitreous humour whose steady rise helps estimate the time since death.

questions.q: During a medico-legal autopsy on a suspected hanging or manual strangulation victim, which anatomical region is deliberately dissected last after draining the cranial and thoracic cavities to avoid artificial blood extravasation?
questions.explain: In suspected neck trauma, the brain and thoracoabdominal organs are removed first to decompress the jugular and subclavian veins, ensuring a bloodless field when dissecting neck muscles and hyoid-laryngeal cartilages so post-mortem Prinsloo-Gordon haemorrhage is not mistaken for ante-mortem bruising.

open.q: Which anatomical region is dissected last in a bloodless field during autopsy of a suspected strangulation or hanging victim?

questions.q: In Nigeria, who holds the legal authority to order the exhumation of a buried corpse when foul play or poisoning is subsequently suspected?
options: The Coroner or a court of competent jurisdiction
The deceased's next of kin alone
questions.explain: Exhumation is strictly regulated by law and requires a formal written order from a Coroner or judicial magistrate/court after an application showing reasonable grounds for medico-legal investigation.

open.q: Which legal authority in Nigeria issues the formal order authorizing the exhumation of a buried body for medico-legal investigation?

questions.q: When exhuming a corpse buried in soil for suspected heavy metal poisoning such as arsenic, which additional environmental sample must be collected alongside visceral tissues?
options: Control soil samples from above, below, and beside the coffin
Surface rainwater collected 1 kilometre away from the cemetery
Bark scrapings from trees outside the burial ground
questions.explain: Because heavy metals like arsenic can naturally occur in soil and leach into a decomposing body (or vice versa), forensic protocol mandates collecting control soil samples from above, below, and around the coffin to rule out post-mortem environmental contamination.

open.q: What non-biological control samples must be collected from the grave during an exhumation for suspected heavy metal poisoning?
accept: Control soil samples around the coffin
Soil from above, below, and beside the coffin
